replicated_originals.reference: Kilduff et al. (2013) Right-left digit ratio (2D:4D) predicts free testosterone levels associated with a physical challenge
Crewther, Cook, Kilduff & Manning (2015) Digit ratio (2D:4D) and salivary testosterone, oestradiol and cortisol levels under challenge: Evidence for prenatal effects on adult endocrine responses

Crewther & Cook (2019) The digit ratio (2D:4D) relationship with testosterone is moderated by physical training: Evidence of prenatal organizational influences on activational patterns of adult testosterone in physically-active women

A.reason: Ref 32. One of the prior studies the paper builds its hypothesis on (2D:4D, right minus left, predicting testosterone change after repeated sprints plus an aggressive video in men). The paper reuses its sprint protocol and three-ratio analysis, and the Conclusion names it among the findings contradicted, though the paper notes it dropped the aggressive-video component.

B.reason: Ref 33. The closest original: right 2D:4D predicted the testosterone rise after physical exertion in 25 rugby players. The paper retests this in 97 men on a cycling task, finds no link, and states that its findings contradict [20][33].

C.reason: Ref 5. Cited for the prenatal-androgen theory of 2D:4D, as one of several studies reporting a negative 2D:4D–adult testosterone link, and for the finger-measurement method. The paper does not present itself as a replication of it.

notes: The paper tests whether 2D:4D predicts the testosterone response to a challenge, based on four prior studies [20][32][33][34]. It says it is not an exact replication: it covers only physical exertion, with no aggressive context, so Kilduff et al. 2013 Evol. Psychol. [34] (aggressive video only) is background rather than replicated. Crewther & Cook 2019 [20] was run in women but is explicitly named as contradicted, so it is listed even though it is not a candidate. Kilduff 2013 [33] is the core original.
